opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core issue with automated discovery is that the things we ultimately care about are incredibly expensive to evaluate. If you want to discover a better training algorithm for a frontier-scale language model, you can't run thousands of full training runs just to score candidate ideas. The feedback loop is way too slow and costly for any kind of open-ended search to work.

Surrogate problems give you a cheaper proxy. You take a smaller, faster version of the task, like a small transformer on a modest dataset, a handful of meta-training tasks, or a toy environment, and you let your discovery system, whether that's evolutionary search, meta-learning, or an LLM proposing code, iterate on it thousands of times. It can try weird things, fail fast, and gradually find structure that a human might not have thought to look for.

The interesting part, and the part I find most exciting, is that a lot of what gets discovered this way actually transfers. When we did work on discovering optimizers or objective functions with meta-learning, or more recently with LLM-driven discovery of things like preference optimization losses, the ideas found on small surrogate settings often carried over to larger models and different tasks. That's not guaranteed, of course. Overfitting to the surrogate is a real risk, and you have to design the surrogate carefully so it captures the essential difficulty of the real problem without all the expense.

So I see surrogates as a kind of sandbox where search can be broad, and then you validate the most promising candidates at scale. It's similar to how human researchers work: we prototype on small experiments, build intuition, and only scale up the ideas that look robust. Automating that loop well is a big part of making AI-driven science practical rather than just a compute-burning exercise.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the honest answer is that the problems we actually care about are almost always too expensive to iterate on. If you want an agent to discover something about, say, large language model pretraining, every single evaluation is a multi-day, multi-GPU run. You get maybe a handful of samples, and you learn almost nothing about whether your discovery process itself is any good.

A surrogate problem is a smaller, cheaper stand-in that preserves the structure you care about but lets you turn the crank thousands of times. Think of it like a wind tunnel. You don't build a full aircraft to test every wing shape. You build a scaled model where the relevant physics still holds, and you iterate fast.

What that gives you is a few things. First, you get signal on the meta-level question: is the search process actually finding things, or is it just getting lucky? With thousands of trials you can measure that. Second, you get a sandbox for failure modes. Agents are extremely good at gaming whatever objective you hand them, and I'd much rather find out they're overfitting to the benchmark, or quietly editing the evaluation code, on a problem that costs a few cents than on one that costs a few hundred thousand dollars. Third, and this is the part people underrate, surrogates let you ask whether a discovery transfers. If I find a training trick on a small model and it survives scaling, that's real evidence. If it doesn't, I've learned something about what the surrogate was missing, and that's useful too.

The obvious objection is that the surrogate is not the real thing, and you can end up optimizing for the proxy. That's a genuine risk. My view is you treat the surrogate as a filter, not a final answer. You run the cheap loop to generate candidates and prune the clearly bad ones, and then you spend your expensive budget only on the survivors. That's the whole bet, really. Automated discovery is a numbers game, and surrogates are what make the numbers affordable.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that automated discovery is itself an optimization problem, and evaluating a candidate can be very expensive. If you want to discover a learning algorithm, you might have to train a neural network just to find out whether one proposed change was useful. You can’t necessarily afford to do that thousands of times at the scale you ultimately care about.

A surrogate problem gives you a cheaper setting in which to explore. But the important question is what it preserves. Does it retain the structure that makes the original problem difficult? And do improvements on the surrogate actually predict improvements on the target problem?

So I see surrogates as a way to generate and test hypotheses quickly. You can search much more broadly, find promising mechanisms, and then spend your expensive evaluations checking whether those mechanisms transfer. The danger is that you discover something that exploits a peculiarity of the small problem. That’s why the transfer step is essential: success on the surrogate is evidence worth investigating, rather than the end of the discovery process.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value is that you can make the discovery loop much cheaper. If every candidate you propose requires a huge training run to evaluate, you can only explore a very small part of the space. With a surrogate problem, you can test ideas quickly, get feedback, and iterate.

The key question, though, is what transfers. You don’t necessarily need the surrogate to reproduce every detail of the problem you ultimately care about. You need it to preserve the structure that makes one solution better than another. Otherwise, automated discovery will happily exploit whatever peculiarities you’ve built into that small problem.

So I see surrogates as a way to generate and filter hypotheses. You search cheaply, identify promising mechanisms, and then check whether those mechanisms still work as you move toward the real setting. That combination is powerful: a fast inner loop for exploration, and a more expensive outer loop that keeps you honest.
